n: Before making any move toward the throne, David asks the Lord for direction. God sends him to Hebron, an ancient city of Judah tied to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

f.g: A city in the hill country of Judah, about 20 miles south of Jerusalem, where the patriarchs were buried.

n: David moves to Hebron with his two wives. Both women connect him to the region of Judah, which would help his acceptance there.

f.g: From Jezreel, a town in Judah (not the northern Jezreel).

n: The loyal band of men who had followed David during his years as a fugitive settle with their families in the towns around Hebron.

f.w: his men that were with him

n: David’s own tribe of Judah publicly anoints him king. This is his second anointing; Samuel had anointed him privately years before. David also learns that the men of Jabesh-gilead risked their lives to bury Saul.

f.g: A town east of the Jordan that Saul had once rescued; its men repaid him by recovering his body.

n: David sends a blessing to Jabesh-gilead, praising their loyalty to Saul. His respect for Saul is sincere, and it also shows Saul’s supporters that he is not their enemy.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — loyal, covenant love; faithful kindness that goes beyond duty.

n: He prays that God will show them the same loyal love and faithfulness, and he promises to repay their kindness himself.

f.g: A common Hebrew pairing (ḥesed and ’emet): steadfast love and faithfulness, qualities especially of God.
Requite = repay.

n: David gently invites them to take courage — Saul is gone, and Judah has a new king. It is a diplomatic hint that they might accept him too.

f.g: Take courage; be strong.

n: Abner, Saul’s cousin and army commander, has other plans. He takes Saul’s surviving son Ish-bosheth to Mahanaim, east of the Jordan, safely away from the Philistines.

f.g: “Man of shame.” He is called Esh-baal (“man of Baal,” meaning master) in 1 Chronicles 8:33; later scribes often replaced “baal” in names with “bosheth” (shame).

n: Abner makes Ish-bosheth king over the northern and eastern tribes. In practice, Abner holds the real power.

f.g: Probably the tribe of Asher (or the Asherites); not the Assyrians.

n: Ish-bosheth’s reign is brief and weak. The nation is now split: the north under Saul’s son, and Judah under David — a preview of the later division of the kingdom.

f.g: The length differs from David’s seven and a half years in Hebron; the extra years may cover the time before Abner established Ish-bosheth.

n: David reigns over Judah from Hebron for seven and a half years before becoming king of all Israel.
The two sides move toward a confrontation. Abner leads Ish-bosheth’s men to Gibeon, a city in Benjamin north of Jerusalem.

f.g: A Benjaminite city about six miles northwest of Jerusalem.

n: Joab, David’s nephew and commander, meets them. The two armies sit facing each other across a large pool — a scene of tense standoff.

f.g: Zeruiah was David’s sister, so Joab and his brothers were David’s nephews.
Archaeologists have found a large rock-cut water shaft at Gibeon (el-Jib) that may be this pool.

n: Abner proposes a contest of champions. “Play” sounds harmless, but it means a deadly combat between chosen young warriors.

f.g: Here a grim euphemism for a combat by champions, perhaps meant to settle the conflict with fewer deaths.

n: Twelve men from each side step forward — twelve Benjaminites for Saul’s house and twelve of David’s men.
Each man grabs his opponent and stabs him, and all twenty-four fall together. The contest settles nothing, and the place is named for the tragedy.

f.g: Hebrew: “field of flints” or “field of blades” (sharp edges).

n: Because the champions’ contest ended in a draw, full battle erupts. David’s men win decisively over Abner’s forces.
Three brothers, sons of David’s sister Zeruiah, are in the battle. The youngest, Asahel, is famous for his speed.

f.g: A gazelle, known for swiftness.

n: Asahel chases Abner himself, determined and single-minded, hoping to kill the enemy commander.

f.w: turned not to the right hand nor to the left
f.g: He kept straight on his target without distraction.

n: Abner, glancing back, recognizes the young man chasing him.
Abner, a veteran warrior, urges Asahel to go after an easier opponent and take his armor as a prize instead. Asahel refuses.

f.g: Here the weapons and gear of a defeated soldier, taken as plunder.

n: Abner pleads again. He doesn’t want to kill Asahel, knowing it would start a blood feud with Joab, Asahel’s powerful brother.

f.w: how then should I hold up my face to Joab
f.g: How could I face Joab? Killing his brother would bring shame and vengeance.

n: When Asahel still won’t stop, Abner thrusts back with the butt end of his spear so hard it goes through him. Everyone who reaches the spot halts in shock.

f.g: The back end of the spear, often pointed so it could be stuck in the ground.
The belly or abdomen.

n: Joab and Abishai keep chasing Abner until sunset, reaching a hill in the wilderness near Gibeon.

f.g: A hill whose exact location is unknown.

n: The Benjaminites, Saul’s own tribe, regroup around Abner on a hilltop, ready to make a stand.
Abner calls for an end to the killing. Fighting fellow Israelites will only leave bitterness, he says — a wise plea, though it also saves his own troops.

f.w: Shall the sword devour for ever?
f.g: A vivid image of war as a beast that never stops eating.
A reminder that both sides are Israelites — this is civil war.

n: Joab swears by God that if Abner had not spoken, the chase would have gone on until morning. He agrees to stop.

f.g: A solemn oath: “as surely as God lives.”

n: Joab sounds the trumpet — the signal to halt — and the fighting ends for that day.

f.g: The shofar, a ram’s horn used to signal troops.

n: Abner’s men march all night, cross the Jordan, and return to their base at Mahanaim.

f.g: Possibly a ravine or region east of the Jordan; the meaning may be “the gorge.”

n: When Joab counts his men, David’s side has lost only nineteen soldiers — plus Asahel, whose death is singled out because it will shape later events.
Abner’s losses are far heavier: 360 men. The battle shows David’s growing strength.

f.g: Threescore = 60; so 360.

n: Asahel is buried in the family tomb in Bethlehem, David’s hometown. Joab marches through the night back to Hebron — carrying a grudge that will lead to Abner’s death in the next chapter.

f.g: A tomb, often cut into rock.
